title: Low-loss deterministic reduction from weighted to unweighted dynamic matching
formal:
Is there a uniform deterministic black-box transformation that converts every explicit fully dynamic \(\alpha\)-approximate maximum-cardinality matching algorithm into a fully dynamic \(\alpha(1-1/q)\)-approximate maximum-weight matching algorithm on general graphs, for every fixed \(\alpha\in(0,1]\) and integer \(q\ge2\), with only an accuracy-dependent polylogarithmic overhead in update time and with preservation of worst-case as well as amortized bounds?

The precise overhead and interfaces are specified below. The transformation must work at the original approximation ratio \(\alpha\); it may not demand a stronger unweighted algorithm with approximation approaching one as \(q\) grows. This card selects the deterministic, fully dynamic version of the source’s broader feature-preserving conversion question. Randomized and partially dynamic extensions are not part of this chosen statement.
why: A low-loss conversion would transfer a broad range of dynamic matching improvements from counting matched edges to optimizing their weights. The central unresolved scope includes algorithms with fixed approximation ratios such as one half or two thirds, not only near-optimal algorithms. Preserving determinism and time guarantees would make the conversion useful across existing algorithmic tradeoffs without redesigning each algorithm.
status_note: The 2022 workshop question, the full 2021 framework PDF (Theorem 3.1 and Remark 3.2), and Bernstein–Chen arXiv:2510.19049v1 (Theorem 6.5 and Section 1.1 limitations) were checked on 2026-09-14; the SIAM publisher confirms the latter’s SODA 2026 publication. The recent reduction is for near-optimal ratios and does not establish the source’s arbitrary-ratio goal or the selected deterministic guarantee. A bounded later-work search found no matching general all-ratio deterministic reduction. The detailed source-grounded variant is complete editorially; its source-open status retains these search and proof-verification limits.

sentences: The question asks for a reusable conversion from dynamic unweighted matching to dynamic weighted matching on general graphs.
An input algorithm with approximation ratio alpha should yield one with ratio alpha times one minus the chosen accuracy.
The selected variant preserves determinism and transfers both worst-case and amortized update guarantees when the input algorithm provides them.
The overhead may depend on accuracy but should be only polylogarithmic in graph size and weight range, apart from the stated auxiliary graph enlargement.
A recent general-graph conversion works for near-optimal input algorithms, leaving the arbitrary-ratio target unresolved.

definitions:
All graphs are finite, undirected, loopless and simple. A matching is a set of edges with pairwise disjoint endpoints. For an unweighted graph \(H\), let \(\nu(H)\) be the maximum number of edges in a matching. An \(\alpha\)-approximation returns a matching \(M\) with \(|M|\ge\alpha\nu(H)\). For a positively weighted graph \(G\), let \(\operatorname{OPT}_w(G)=\max_M\sum_{e\in M}w(e)\). The weighted output must satisfy
\[\sum_{e\in M}w(e)\ge\alpha(1-1/q)\operatorname{OPT}_w(G).\]
The empty graph has optimum zero.

Both problems start with an empty graph on a fixed labelled vertex set. Updates insert an absent edge or delete a present edge, in any order. Weighted insertions additionally specify an integer weight in \([W]\), for a supplied integer \(W\ge1\). A weight change can be expressed as deletion followed by insertion. No bipartiteness or sparsity promise is imposed. Updates are revealed sequentially and may depend on earlier outputs, since the chosen algorithms are deterministic. Weights, vertex labels, \(W\) and \(q\) are represented in binary.

The input subroutine \(A\) has a uniform finite program, initializes an empty unweighted graph, and supports edge insertion and deletion. It stores an explicit current matching: a mate lookup is constant-time and its edge list can be enumerated in time proportional to its length plus one. Each update supplies the list of matching edges inserted or removed during that update, and the cost of producing that list is included in \(A\)'s update time. Thus changes of output are charged, as required by the recourse condition in the 2021 source. The transformation can create independent instances of \(A\), call their operations and inspect their reported matchings; it cannot inspect their implementation or hidden state. Only their \(\alpha\)-approximation promise may be used, so the guarantee must survive every valid choice of approximate matching by the subroutine. The transformed algorithm also maintains its weighted matching explicitly and charges every output change.

Here is the required overhead. There must be one transformation, one total computable function \(F:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and one fixed exponent \(b\ge0\), independent of \(\alpha\) and \(A\). For a weighted sequence on \(n\ge2\) vertices with at most \(m\) edges present at any time, put
\[N=\lceil F(q)n\rceil,\quad D=\min\{\binom{N}{2},\lceil F(q)(m+n)\rceil\},\quad L=F(q)(1+\log_2(n+2)+\log_2(W+1))^b.\]
Let \(I_A(N)\ge N\) be any nondecreasing upper bound on empty-graph initialization time of \(A\). Let \(U_A(N,D)\ge1\) be any upper bound, nondecreasing in both arguments, on its update time for sequences with at most \(N\) vertices and \(D\) edges. The weighted algorithm must initialize within \(L(I_A(N)+n)\) operations and have update bound
\[L\bigl(U_A(N,D)+1\bigr).\]
If \(U_A\) is a worst-case per-update bound, this must be a worst-case weighted bound. If it is only an amortized bound, every weighted prefix of \(T\) updates must cost at most \(TL(U_A(N,D)+1)\), excluding the separately charged initialization. These are implications for each applicable bound, not a requirement to turn an amortized input guarantee into a worst-case output guarantee. Multiplicative constants may be absorbed into \(F\). No polynomial dependence on \(q\) is required: it is an accuracy parameter, and the source’s bipartite blueprint already allows a larger dependence.

Use a word-RAM with \(\Theta(\log_2(nWF(q)+2))\)-bit words, with a fixed sufficiently large constant multiplier. Word memory accesses, comparisons, branches, Boolean operations, shifts, modular addition/subtraction/multiplication and quotient/remainder by a nonzero word have unit cost. Both subroutine calls and all surrounding work are charged; the subroutine is evaluated in the same word model. The transformation may use at most \(\lceil L\rceil\) simultaneous instances, each on at most \(N\) vertices and \(D\) edges, and auxiliary memory bounded by \(F(q)(n+\log_2(W+1)+2)^d\) words for one fixed exponent \(d\). Its state has no uncharged graph-dependent advice. The bound is uniform over every finite update sequence and over the given \(W\); using unit-weight graphs as oracle instances does not give their answers for free.

The explicit overhead formalizes an accuracy-dependent enlargement of the auxiliary graph and a polylogarithmic factor in size and weight range. Allowing \(m+n\) in the edge bound accommodates auxiliary vertices and edges; it does not promise exact preservation of sparse graph size. These bookkeeping choices and the deterministic restriction are editorial specifications of the source’s requested type of transformation.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of this uniform transformation and overhead parameters. A positive proof must cover every admissible approximation factor and subroutine, preserve its deterministic correctness, and establish the stated transfer of both kinds of time guarantee when applicable. A result requiring \(\alpha\) to approach one with \(q\), a constant multiplicative loss bounded away from one, or a conversion only for bipartite weighted graphs is insufficient. A weighted algorithm unrelated to the supplied subroutine does not establish the black-box theorem merely because it is polynomial-time. Failure of one particular transformation is not a refutation of the existence claim.

context_blocks.text: The source asks for a general-graph analogue of the bipartite reduction, with little loss in approximation and update complexity. Its broader discussion also includes randomized and partially dynamic settings. This card isolates the deterministic fully dynamic feature-preserving statement and records its explicit interface and overhead.

Theorem 3.1 of Bernstein–Dudeja–Langley gives the desired \(\alpha\mapsto(1-\varepsilon)\alpha\) conversion on bipartite graphs, with accuracy-dependent graph enlargement and logarithmic weight-range dependence. Remark 3.2 explains why explicit matching output provides the recourse bound required by the conversion.

Bernstein and Chen’s SODA 2026 result gives a low-loss conversion for general weighted graphs when the unweighted algorithm already has approximation \(1-\varepsilon_0\), where \(\varepsilon_0\) must be polynomially smaller than the desired error. Theorem 6.5 is randomized and amortized.

The later paper’s limitations discussion explicitly says that its result cannot transfer arbitrary fixed approximation ratios with small loss, and retains that more general conversion as the desired goal. Thus its title and near-optimal result do not resolve the all-ratio deterministic statement selected here.
